planting.note: Set divisions or container plants in spring into humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in partial shade; this larger, more vigorous native selection has bronzy-red dissected foliage and improved resistance to the leaf-spotting that troubles the species.

directions: Huggy Bear is a selected form of the eastern native wild geranium, chosen for its warm bronzy-red, finely cut foliage and sprays of clear pink flowers that open over the woodland floor in mid-spring. It spreads gradually into a tidy clump rather than running aggressively, making it a good companion for ferns, hostas, and other shade perennials along a wooded path or border. Give it morning sun with afternoon shade in warmer climates, since both flower display and leaf color fade where summers are hottest and driest. Deer and rabbits generally leave it alone, and the flowers draw in early-season native bees.

planting.note: Set purchased transplants out after frost danger has passed into moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; part of the Glimmer series bred for fully double, rose-like blooms and strong resistance to impatiens downy mildew.

directions: Glimmer Strawberry Sparkler covers itself in small, fully double, rose-form blooms splashed in red and white, held over a mounded, self-cleaning plant that needs no deadheading. Its main advance over older double impatiens is strong resistance to the downy mildew pathogen that devastated impatiens plantings over the last decade, making this a far more reliable choice for deep shade beds and hanging baskets. Keep soil evenly moist and feed every couple of weeks through the season to sustain the heavy bloom count. It performs best tucked out of hot midday sun, where the papery flowers and foliage hold up longest.

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or container stock in spring into moist, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to sun; Princess Elsa spreads quickly by stolons into a low, dense mat of ruffled, metallic silvery-green foliage.

directions: Princess Elsa forms a fast-spreading carpet of frosted, silvery-green rosettes that catch the light in a shaded border, topped in late spring by short spikes of violet-blue flowers that pollinators visit readily. Like other bugleweeds it is largely untroubled by deer and rabbits and needs no deadheading or regular feeding once settled. In the Gulf South, site it where it gets relief from the hottest afternoon sun and keep the shallow roots from drying out, since both heat and drought stress can thin the mat; good air movement also helps avoid crown rot in humid summers. Use it to edge shaded paths or underplant deciduous shrubs where its reflective foliage brightens dim corners.

common_name: Heart to Heart Creme Brulee Caladium

planting.note: Plant tubers after the last frost once soil has warmed to at least 65°F, 1-2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; a Heart to Heart series introduction prized for leaf color that holds steady from spring through fall.

directions: Creme Brulee carries large, heart-shaped leaves washed in creamy white with a soft pink-bronze border that blends gently toward the center, laced with fine white veining for a painterly, refined look. Unlike some caladiums that shift color as the season progresses, this one holds its pattern consistently from spring planting through fall decline, which makes it easy to plan companion plantings around. Keep the soil consistently moist and avoid setting tubers out while the ground is still cool, since chilly spring soil will stunt and discolor new growth. It works equally well massed in a shaded bed, in a container on a covered porch, or brought indoors as a houseplant before frost.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants once frost danger has passed into rich, well-drained, consistently moist potting mix or garden soil in partial shade; a free-flowering, heat-tolerant Ball FloraPlant selection bred for strong garden and trial performance in warm climates.

directions: Blue Radiance produces an early, steady flush of blue-and-red pendant blooms over a strong, upright-mounding habit that resists splitting apart the way many basket fuchsias do under heavy flower weight. It has notably better heat tolerance than older fuchsia cultivars, which lets it hold up through warm, humid Southern springs and summers where fuchsias often falter and drop buds. Keep the potting mix or bed evenly moist and feed regularly to sustain the long bloom window, and position it where it gets protection from intense midday sun. It is best treated as a tender annual outside the mildest climates and is well suited to hanging baskets, window boxes, and large shaded containers.

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated starts after all frost danger has passed into moist, well-drained, fertile soil or containers in partial shade to sun; part of the University of Florida-bred Down Town series, which tolerates both sun and shade better than many older coleus.

directions: NYC Nights carries dark maroon-burgundy foliage flecked with gold and chartreuse speckles, giving it strong visual contrast whether it's grown in a bright border or a shadier container planting. It was bred through the University of Florida's coleus program and commercialized as part of the Down Town series, which was selected for holding its color and compact habit across a wider range of light levels than most older coleus cultivars. Pinch stem tips regularly to keep the plant full and bushy, and remove flower spikes as they form so the plant's energy stays directed into foliage rather than seed production. Give it consistently moist, fertile soil and it will hold its color and habit from spring planting until the first fall frost.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — UF Coleus Breeding Program
